Open one level at a time. **Hint 1** gives the conceptual direction, **Hint 2** the SQL technique, **Hint 3** the query structure, and the final level is in [`solutions/`](../solutions/).

## M0-E01 · Peek at the first five books

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

You only want a few rows. Which clause caps the number of rows returned?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

`SELECT ... FROM ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT n`. ORDER BY makes "first" well-defined.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`SELECT "title", "year" FROM "books" ORDER BY "id" LIMIT ...;`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M0.md#m0-e01).

## M0-E03 · Artworks with no acquisition date

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

NULL means "no value". Comparing anything to NULL with `=` never yields true.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

SQL has a special operator for testing NULL.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`... WHERE "acquired" IS NULL;`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M0.md#m0-e03).

## M0-E05 · Tally raw votes

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

You want one row per distinct title, with a count.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

`GROUP BY "title"` with `COUNT("title")`.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`SELECT "title", COUNT("title") FROM "votes" GROUP BY "title";`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M0.md#m0-e05).

## M0-E06 · Average rating per book

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

Many ratings per book become one row per book, so you need a grouping.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

`AVG(...)` inside `ROUND(..., 2)`, then `AS "rating"`, then `GROUP BY "book_id"`.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`SELECT "book_id", ROUND(AVG("rating"), 2) AS "rating" FROM "ratings" GROUP BY ...;`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M0.md#m0-e06).

## M0-E08 · Fernanda Melchor's books, with nested subqueries

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

Work inside-out. First her id (authors), then her book ids (authored), then their titles (books).

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

The middle step can return several rows, so the outer filter needs `IN (...)`.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`SELECT "title" FROM "books" WHERE "id" IN (SELECT "book_id" FROM "authored" WHERE "author_id" = (SELECT "id" FROM "authors" WHERE ...));`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M0.md#m0-e08).

## M0-E09 · Author names next to book titles, with JOIN

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

`authors` has names and `books` has titles. They connect through `authored`.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

Two JOINs, each matching a primary key with a foreign key.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`FROM "authors" JOIN "authored" ON "authors"."id" = "authored"."author_id" JOIN "books" ON ...`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M0.md#m0-e09).

## D0-01 · The NULL that never matches

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

What is the result of `NULL = NULL` in SQL? Is it true?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

Comparisons with NULL produce NULL (unknown), and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

Use the operator built for NULL tests.

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M0.md#d0-01).

## D0-02 · Joined on the wrong column

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

Read each ON clause aloud. Does it connect a primary key to the matching foreign key?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

`authors.id` is an *author* id. Which column of `authored` holds author ids?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

The first ON should use `authored.author_id`.

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M0.md#d0-02).

## D0-03 · Duplicate rows from a one-to-many join

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

How many rows of `ratings` match one book?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

A JOIN outputs one row per *matching pair*, so a book with 20 ratings appears 20 times.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

Collapse the duplicates with `DISTINCT` or `GROUP BY "books"."id"`, or use `WHERE "id" IN (SELECT "book_id" FROM "ratings")`.

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M0.md#d0-03).

## D0-04 · One average instead of one per book

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

Without grouping, an aggregate collapses the *whole table* into one row.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

Which column defines "per book"?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

Add `GROUP BY "book_id"`.

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M0.md#d0-04).

## D0-05 · `=` with a subquery that returns many rows

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

How many rows does the middle subquery return?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

`= (subquery)` in SQLite silently uses only the **first** row.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

Use the set-membership operator.

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M0.md#d0-05).

## D0-06 · Grouped by the wrong column

<details><summary>Hint 1 · direction</summary>

Each group becomes one output row. How many distinct ids are there?

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 2 · technique</summary>

Group by what you want one row *per*.

</details>

<details><summary>Hint 3 · structure</summary>

`GROUP BY "year"`

</details>

Final: [solution](../solutions/M0.md#d0-06).
